tone_statements.citation: Akinbo, Samuel & Dalhatu Abigail Musa. 2025. Acoustics of level tones in Gbagyi. Paper (slides, 33 pp.) presented at the Linguistic Society of America Annual Meeting, Philadelphia, January 2025.
tone_statements.quote: Gbagyi is a tone language, which means pitch contrasts bring about distinctions in meaning (Yip, 2002). The language contrast four level tones (Dalhatu 2017, 2021). Low (L) gà “to give” Mid (M) gā “to scatter” High (H) gá “near?” Super High (S) ga̋ “near” [...] Gbagyi also has two contour tones. [...] The results of this work support H, M, L and S as the lexically contrastive level tones in Gbagyi (in line with Dalhatu 2017, 2021).
tone_statements.locator: slides 6-7 ('Tone inventory: level tones', 'contour tones') and slide 27 ('Discussion and conclusion')
tone_statements.n_tones: 4 level (L, M, H, Super-high) + 2 contour (H-L fall, S-L fall)

tone_statements.citation: Dalhatu, Abigail Musa. 2019. Gbagyi syllable and phonotactics. Journal of the Nigerian Languages Project 1: 19-36.
tone_statements.quote: However, of equal importance is the mention of the fact that Gbagyi has both register and contour tones, with four register tones (Super high, High, Mid and Low) and two contour tones (Super-high rising and High falling). It must be noted that while all other tones are marked using some conventional annotations, the Mid-tone is generally left unmarked.

tone_statements.n_tones: 4 register (Super-high, H, M, L) + 2 contour (Super-high rising, High falling)

tone_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. & Daniel J. Magaji. 1970. Essentials of Gwari grammar. Occasional Publication 27, Institute of African Studies, University of Ibadan. 166 pp.
tone_statements.quote: 14. There are three basic tones in Gwari: low [...], mid [...] and high [...]. Monosyllabic verb stems bear one of these three tones. [...] In addition, a fourth level tone slightly lower than mid, as well as a rising tone [...] and a falling tone [...] are found. Absence of any tone mark indicates lower-mid tone. 15. The three basic tones undergo various modifications in certain tonal environments. Nouns generally consist of two syllables and will serve as illustrations. After a low tone syllable, mid tone becomes lower-mid, while high tone becomes rising tone. A second low tone remains low.
tone_statements.locator: p. 14, Chapter Three 'The Tone System', secs. 14-15
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.n_tones: 3 basic level (L, M, H) + derived lower-mid level + rising and falling contours

sources.note: No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the article. Para. 6: 'Gwari operates a terraced level three-tone system having low (L), mid (M) and high (H) tones (Hyman & Magaji 1971:15) as well as downdrift and downstep'; H realised as rising after L, L as falling after M/H; downstepped M and H.

sources.citation: Muhammad, Aliyu Busa. 2012. A comparative study of Hausa and Gbagyi sound systems. PhD dissertation, Department of African Languages and Cultures, Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria. 136 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on Gbagyi stress. Tone sections 2.2.5.3 (pp. 64-65) and 4.1.4 (pp. 82-83): Gbagyi has H, L, M and falling tone patterns (Hyman & Magaji 1970 five tones; Sanda 1986 three; author proposes four). The only occurrence of 'stress' is a general remark (pp. 16-17) that tone, vowel structure, stress and syllabification 'might have been illusive' to non-native authors of earlier Gbagyi books.

sources.citation: Akinbo, Samuel & Dalhatu Abigail Musa. 2025. Acoustics of level tones in Gbagyi. Paper (slides, 33 pp.) presented at the Linguistic Society of America Annual Meeting, Philadelphia, January 2025.
sources.quote: Gbagyi is a tone language, which means pitch contrasts bring about distinctions in meaning (Yip, 2002). The language contrast four level tones (Dalhatu 2017, 2021). Low (L) gà “to give” Mid (M) gā “to scatter” High (H) gá “near?” Super High (S) ga̋ “near” [...] Gbagyi also has two contour tones. sources.locator: slides 6-7 ('Tone inventory: level tones', 'contour tones') and slide 27 ('Discussion and conclusion')
sources.note: First-hand acoustic study (5 speakers, F0 of disyllables): Gbagyi contrasts four level tones L, M, H and Super-high (S), unrestricted co-occurrence in disyllables, plus two contour tones (HL fall, S-L fall) restricted to long vowels / non-initial syllables; results support S as a fourth level higher than H (Dalhatu 2017, 2021) rather than Hyman & Magaji's lower-mid; H and S surface rising after L (tone transfer per Hyman & Magaji 1970); M pitch varies with neighbouring tones.

tone.says: Chapter Three 'The Tone System' (pp. 14-28, secs. 14-28): three basic tones L, M, H on monosyllabic verb stems; in addition a fourth level 'lower-mid' (analysed as a mid lowered by a preceding, often no longer audible, low tone, which then resets the reference pitch for following mids = downstep-like register lowering), plus rising (L+H -> L-rising) and falling (H/M+L -> falling) contours derived by tone spreading; rules for contour simplification before H/M, floating low-tone effects, tonal no…

sources.note: Per Adeniyi & Elugbe 2018's citations: instrumental study of downstep in Gwari's three-tone (H, M, L) terraced system - downstepped mid also perceived as a raised L by some speakers (fn.6); contour simplification yields downstepped H (pp.122-125); voiceless obstruents are tone raisers: H and M measured 5 Hz and 7.9 Hz higher after voiceless than voiced fricatives, M 9.2 Hz higher after voiceless stops (p.129); tonal morphemes ('tomorphs') in associative constructions.
